extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners studying peer review systems (ML/NLP researchers, conference organizers, peer-review scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, running, and analyzing simulations of conference-style peer review using LLM-powered agents to study factors that affect review quality and decisions. The work targets investigating reviewer characteristics, area-chair behavior, and mechanism variants (rebuttal, numeric ratings) in a conference pipeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer dimensions: Commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Commitment refers to the reviewer’s dedication and sense of responsibility in engaging with the manuscript. This involves a proactive and careful approach to provide thorough and constructive feedback on submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commitment influences review length, depth, and post-rebuttal engagement; AGENTREVIEW models reviewers as responsible versus irresponsible and reports effects such as altruism fatigue (one irresponsible reviewer can reduce overall commitment by 18.7%) and shorter review texts (irresponsible reviews 22.2% shorter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer dimensions: Intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Intention describes the motivation behind the reviews, focusing on whether the reviewer aims to genuinely help authors improve their papers or is influenced by biases or conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorize reviewers as benign versus malicious. Malicious reviewers disproportionately cite lack of novelty and can create bimodal rating distributions and negative spillover effects on other reviewers' scores. Consider conflict theory implications (competitive behavior leading to low ratings for competing papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer dimensions: Knowledgeability
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledgeability measures the reviewer’s expertise in the manuscript’s subject area (knowledgeable vs unknowledgeable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert reviewers identify technical issues and experimental validation more often (6.8% more critiques on experiments), while less-knowledgeable reviewers more often note insufficient discussion of limitations (24% more). Imperfect assignment and expanding reviewer pools can degrade expertise matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured review format (four sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should comprise four sections: significance and novelty, potential reasons for acceptance, potential reasons for rejection, and suggestions for improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This format is aligned with conventional ML/NLP conference review structures and is required of LLM agents in AGENTREVIEW (Liang et al. protocol). It supports content-level analyses and generation of 4 reasons to accept/reject per paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeric overall rating (1–10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each reviewer provides a numerical rating from 1 to 10 for the paper (unless the nonumeric-rating mechanism is used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numeric ratings serve as a decision shortcut for area chairs; removing numeric ratings (nonumericrating setting) significantly changes decision overlap with baseline (Jaccard index 0.20), indicating ratings strongly influence final outcomes and can induce anchoring bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-phase review pipeline
rubrics_metrics.description: The peer review process is modeled as five phases: I. Reviewer Assessment; II. Author-Reviewer Discussion (rebuttal); III. Reviewer-AC Discussion; IV. Meta-review Compilation; V. Paper Decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each phase has specific visibility and interaction rules: Phase I reviewers see only paper+own assessment; Phase II authors rebut; Phase III reviewers reconsider and update ratings; Phase IV AC synthesizes; Phase V AC makes decision. These phases are the backbone of simulation and evaluation of mechanism variants (e.g., no-rebuttal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Area Chair (AC) roles and styles
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs facilitate reviewer discussions, synthesize feedback into meta-reviews, and make final decisions. Three AC involvement styles: authoritarian, conformist, and inclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoritarian ACs prioritize their own judgments (may skew decisions; lower correlation with baseline). Conformist ACs rely heavily on reviewers' evaluations (high semantic overlap but risk lack of independent judgment). Inclusive ACs consider all discussion, rebuttals, and their expertise to make balanced decisions and align most closely with baseline outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data selection criteria for papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers chosen for simulation should: (1) be from conferences with international impact and significant academic relevance; (2) be publicly available; (3) reflect real-world distribution including accepted and rejected papers; (4) span a broad time range to mitigate evolving reviewer preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AGENTREVIEW selects ICLR submissions (2020–2023) and uses stratified sampling across categories (oral/spotlight/poster/rejection) to produce a dataset that mirrors real-world paper quality distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline experimental setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a baseline with no specific reviewer characteristics for LLM agents to serve as a consistent reference when testing the impact of individual variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The baseline enables measuring changes caused by introducing responsible/irresponsible, benign/malicious, or knowledgeable/unknowledgeable reviewers. AGENTREVIEW generates statistics (10,460 reviews, etc.) under baseline for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed acceptance rate for decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Simulate AC decision-making with a fixed acceptance rate of 32% to reflect realistic conference acceptance behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each AC is assigned batches (10 papers) and asked to accept 3–4 papers per batch, constraining decision-making and enabling comparison to real-conference acceptance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer characteristic prompting as fixed traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer types (knowledgeable/unknowledgeable, responsible/irresponsible, benign/malicious) are instantiated via detailed prompts and treated as fixed characteristics in the simulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompts describing reviewer behavior are provided (Appendix Figure 10). This controlled assignment allows isolation of individual latent variables' effects on outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author rebuttal expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors respond to initial reviews with rebuttals addressing misunderstandings, justifying methodologies, and acknowledging valid critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AGENTREVIEW models rebuttal phase (Phase II) but finds rebuttals have less significant impact than reviewer features—possibly due to anchoring bias or uniform quality improvements during rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism variants to test (no-rebuttal, nonumericrating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate alternative peer review mechanisms: (1) no-rebuttal (remove Phase II and III interactions); (2) nonumericrating (omit numeric ratings so AC decisions rely solely on review content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No-rebuttal has minimal impact on final decisions in simulation; removing numeric ratings drastically alters accepted paper sets (low overlap with baseline), indicating mechanism design critically affects outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement and similarity metrics for evaluating decisions and meta-reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Jaccard Index, Cohen’s Kappa, Percentage Agreement to compare final decision sets; use BERTScore and sentence-embedding similarity to quantify alignment between reviews and meta-reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics are applied to measure how different settings diverge from the baseline and to quantify semantic alignment between reviewers and AC meta-reviews (e.g., inclusive ACs show highest alignment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-level categorization of accept/reject reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze and categorize textual reasons for acceptance and rejection across reviewer types to understand qualitative differences (e.g., malicious reviewers focus on lack of novelty; benign reviewers focus on scalability/practicality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use content analysis to detect patterns (length, focus). Example: malicious reviews more frequently mention lack of novelty (10.4% of feedback) vs benign (3.69%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer assignment and expertise matching
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer-paper assignment should attempt to match expertise but acknowledge assignments are often imperfect or random; mismatches affect review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulations should incorporate imperfect assignment realities; consider exploring counterfactuals and varying assignment policies to study impacts (cited works: Saveski et al., Xu et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling across paper categories (stratified sampling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select papers via stratified sampling across acceptance categories (oral/top5%, spotlight/top25%, poster, rejection) to include diverse quality levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures simulated reviewer behavior is evaluated across realistic quality distributions and avoids bias toward only accepted papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction to generate multiple accept/reject reasons per paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask LLM reviewers to generate multiple (four) reasons to accept or reject each paper, following prior evaluation protocols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides richer signal for content-level evaluation and permits alignment checks with human reviews (AGENTREVIEW reports 90%/77%/39% papers with 2/3/4 points aligned with human reviewers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Area Chair decision process and synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs should integrate Phase I–III discussions, their own observations, and numeric ratings into a meta-review that synthesizes strengths and weaknesses and guides the final decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-reviews include synthesized assessments and a numeric meta-score; AC style (inclusive/authoritarian/conformist) affects semantic similarity to reviewers and final decision alignment with baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation protocol for realism of LLM-generated reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess realism by sampling papers and matching major comments between human and LLM-generated reviews using extraction tools (e.g., LlamaIndex), checking overlap counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AGENTREVIEW measured alignment (2/3/4 out of 4 accept/reject points) and qualitative unique insights from LLMs; use such protocols to validate simulated review authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and privacy considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about the sensitivity of real peer review data; preserve reviewer privacy and avoid using LLMs as replacement for human reviewers without oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AGENTREVIEW generates simulated data to avoid privacy issues. The authors explicitly advise against replacing human reviewers with LLMs in real-world peer review and recommend human oversight due to LLM imperfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations to note when using LLM agents
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs cannot dynamically generate new empirical data in response to reviewer comments and may not capture nuanced human judgments; analyses often isolate single variables rather than multi-way interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document these limitations when interpreting simulation results; consider future integration of specialized sub-models or mixture-of-experts to improve realism.
